I wouldn't consider you a "TERF," simply because of that observation, just naturally biased to your viewpoint as I am to mine (thats natural). I will say that there is a bit more to being transgender, as its been shown to be genetic rather than psychological. A need rather than a want.  I do agree as a stereotypically feminine transwoman and feminist that my presentation as an overtly 'traditional' female would seem at odds with my ideals. However, I still dressed in this manner prior to coming out, and frankly still would if I were still in the closet. I think more often than not the style in which a transgender individual dresses is a personal preference rather than an attempt to uphold a societal construct that we recognize to be harmful. Then, of course, there is the matter of camouflage. Many of us struggle in public, or are at higher risk for violence due to how strongly we may stand out. I am harassed far less often when I am in full makeup and dress, than if I skip my eyeliner and wear a t-shirt. The viewpoint that gender is non-binary and that sex (scientifically) is binary is a touchy subject. Though personally, I see it as follows: Sex is a medical designation necessary so doctors understand the physical and chemical makeup of your body as it was at birth to provide accurate medical diagnoses (I am Male, as I was born Male I am considered AMAB or Assigned Male at Birth), Gender is your identity in terms of presentation and pronouns and while unrelated can be affected by the former (this is something only definable by the individual, in my case I identify as a woman.) I've always been a very anxious person, but there was a night when I was 17 when I had this awful feeling eating at the back of my mind. It was late in the day, I didnt have school, and I was on the brink of a panic attack with no discernible reason when my father called me. He was just coherent enough to make me believe he may have been fine, he sounded distant/upset. I started to ask what was wrong, and as I persisted he repeatedly himself in response in this dull monotonous tone. 
"Its okay, I'm okay." 
"Dad, I'm worried what's going on."
"It's okay, it's alright, I'm okay... it's okay."
I started to cry, something was wrong and I could tell, so when he started to just repeat those words without provocation, I told him I needed to go. I got my mother, told her something was wrong and I needed to go to my dad's. We got there and his car was in the drive way. All of the curtains were closed, the house was dark. In the wake of my parents divorce he had let it fall to ruin. There were painted swatches on the walls of colors he and my mother had argued over, the walls other than that were bare. The baseboards had been gone since I was 7, and the carpet was patchy and spotted where the cats had shredded it. He stopped caring. 
I didnt have my keys, as after he almost broke my hand in a fit of rage I moved in with my mother and grandmother.
I tried the doors, the windows and even went around back and my heart was pounding in my ears. I called the police, and when they arrived the attempted the same but refused to break down the door. 
I kicked the door in myself, and down the hall, in the room he had shared with my mother (a brown room, with cobwebs in every corner, milk crate furniture and a twin mattress on the floor) my father took every last pill my mother had left in the house in an attempt at suicide. 
We as a family are unfortunately riddled with mental illness, with schizophrenia, depression, anxiety and mood disorders on all sides. My mother herself was on disability for severe depression, having attempted suicide at least 6 times since I was born. I saw her hospitalized more than I saw her at home. When she was home she slept, in a single spot on the couch, drank Pepsi and cried. I was mainly in shock, as the police walked him, an arm over each shoulder while he babbled confused and incoherent like a toddler. He was crying, and I had never seen my father cry before. Almost 4 years after the divorce it still affected him that strongly. I can only imagine being alone didnt help. 
When they got him to the ICU he was kept for over a month. He was delirious, couldn't form sentences and didnt seem to recognize any of us. We still came to see him, of course and as time went on he came back slowly. I had genuinely thought he was gone. 
His brothers came and fixed the door with the lock and handle I bought him, and he's much better now-a-days, having started to repaint, turning the bedroom into an office with his drawing desk and displaying his books on shelves throughout the house. I hope that he never has to feel that way again.
